info.name: Material Master API (PostgreSQL + RBAC)
info.description:
Material master backend — NestJS + PostgreSQL, JWT auth, role-based access control.

## Conventions

- Base URL is `{{baseUrl}}` (default `http://localhost:3000/api`).
- Uploaded images are served from `{{fileBaseUrl}}/uploads/...`, **outside** the `/api` prefix.
- Storage is PostgreSQL. The database, its tables and the four demo accounts are created on first boot.
- All bodies are JSON.
- Validation errors come back as `{ "errors": { "fieldName": "message" } }` with status 400.
- Delete guards come back as `{ "reason": "..." }` with status 409.
- Successful DELETE returns 204 with no body.
- **Every request needs a bearer token.** Run one of the four logins in **Auth (start here)** first; it stores the token in `{{token}}` and the collection sends it automatically. Without one you get `401`; with the wrong role you get `403`.

## Hierarchy

```
category --< subcategory --< subcategory --< ... --< material
```

Categories and sub-categories are separate resources. Sub-categories **nest inside each other with no depth limit** via `parentId`.

Seeded example, 3 levels deep:

```
Steel & Metals            (category 1)
  Pipes                   (sub-category 2, parentId null)
    Square Hollow Section (sub-category 3, parentId 2)
```

**Placing a sub-category** — send `parentId` to nest it, or `categoryId` to put it at the top of a category:

- `parentId` alone → `categoryId` is derived from the parent.
- Both → they must agree, or 400.
- `categoryId` alone → sits directly under the category (`parentId: null`).

Every sub-category response carries `depth` and `path` (category name first), so you can render a tree without walking `parentId` yourself.

**Placing a material** — same idea, and it can hang off a sub-category at any depth:

- `subcategoryId` alone → `categoryId` is derived.
- Both → must agree, or 400.
- `categoryId` alone → sits directly under the category.

## Chaining

Create requests save the new record's id into collection variables (`categoryId`, `subcategoryId`, `childId`, `materialId`), so the GET/PUT/DELETE requests below them work without editing anything. Run the folders top to bottom.

## Register

See the **Register (new user)** folder. `POST /auth/register` takes the whole "Add New User" form as `multipart/form-data` — first/last name, email, phone, password, role, status, departments, project assignment, reporting-to, plus a profile image and a digital signature.

Public sign-up defaults to `viewer` and cannot request `admin`. The admin-only `POST /users` takes the same body with no such limit.

## RBAC

Four seeded accounts, **all with the password `123456`**:

| Email | Role | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `suhana@gmail.com` | `admin` | everything, plus the user directory |
| `category@gmail.com` | `category_manager` | **adds categories and sub-categories** |
| `material@gmail.com` | `material_manager` | **adds materials** |
| `viewer@gmail.com` | `viewer` | read-only |

Those four are **seeded rows in the `roles` table**, not hardcoded. Add your own in **Roles & Permissions** and it works everywhere a role is accepted.

Permissions are named `module:action` (`category:create`, `material:delete`, …)
and live in the `role_permissions` table — one row per role per module, four
toggles wide. Controllers ask for permissions, never for roles, so re-cutting
a role is a change in the **Roles & Permissions** screen, not in the code.

Because the guards read them per request, a toggle applies to already-issued
tokens on their very next call.

| | admin | category_manager | material_manager | viewer |
| --- | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| read categories / sub-categories / materials | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| write categories + sub-categories | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| write materials | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| manage users | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

A denied request answers `403` and names what was missing:

```json
{
  "statusCode": 403,
  "error": "Forbidden",
  "message": "Your role 'category_manager' is not allowed to perform this action",
  "requiredPermissions": "material:create",
  "role": "category_manager"
}
```

### Suggested run order

1. **Auth > Login as Category Manager** → run the **Categories** and **Sub-categories** folders.
2. **Auth > Login as Material Manager** → run the **Materials** folder.
3. **Auth > Login as Admin** → run the **Users** folder.
4. **Auth > Login as Viewer** → every write in any folder now answers 403.

The `(403)` requests at the bottom of each folder pin a specific role's
token, so they demonstrate the denial no matter who is currently signed in.

item.name: Roles & Permissions
item.description:
**Roles are database rows, not an enum in the code.** Creating "Site Engineer" here immediately makes `site_engineer` a role a user can be given, and the grid you submit for it is what the guards check.

### The grid

One row per module, four toggles wide — READ / WRITE / UPDATE / DELETE. Each toggle that is on becomes a `module:action` permission string:

| Toggle | Permission |
| --- | --- |
| READ | `material:read` |
| WRITE | `material:create` |
| UPDATE | `material:update` |
| DELETE | `material:delete` |

A module with **no row** is simply not configured for the role — that is what the trash icon does, as opposed to turning all four toggles off.

### It applies immediately

Permissions are read per request, so flipping a toggle changes what an already-issued token can do on its **very next call**. Nobody has to log back in. Same for moving a user to a different role.

Run **Auth > Login as Admin** first — every route here needs `role:*`.

request.description:
The left-hand list. Each role carries its `color` swatch, `userCount` (how many people hold it) and `moduleCount` (rows in its grid).

Saves the first non-system role into `{{roleId}}`.

Everything the grid can switch on, with the grey `group` label above each name. Only modules with real guarded routes are listed, so no toggle is decorative.

Saves the Materials module into `{{moduleId}}`.
The eleven swatches on "IDENTIFY WITH COLOR". Any valid `#RRGGBB` is accepted when creating a role — this list is only what the UI paints.

The "Create New Role" dialog: a name and a colour.

The slug the JWT will carry is derived from the name — `Site Engineer` becomes `site_engineer`. A **new role holds no permissions at all** until you submit its grid.

Saves the id into `{{roleId}}`.

**400** on a duplicate name, on two names that collapse to the same slug, or on a colour that is not hex.

item.name: Get a role + its Configured Permissions

request.description: The right-hand panel. `permissions` is the grid as rendered — one row per module with the four booleans. `grants` is the same thing flattened into the permission strings the guards actually compare, which is handy when you are debugging a 403.

Adds a single row to the grid. Re-posting the same `moduleId` updates that row rather than failing, so it doubles as "flip one toggle".

Omitted booleans default to false (`read` defaults to true).

The SUBMIT PERMISSIONS button. **The posted list becomes the entire grid** — any module you leave out is removed from the role.

Takes effect on the next request from anyone holding this role, with no re-login.

**409** if you try to strip the built-in Admin role of read+update on Users or Roles — that would lock everyone out of permissions for good.

Un-configures that module for the role entirely — different from turning its four toggles off, though the effect on access is the same.

**404** if the module was not configured for this role to begin with.

Full replace of the role card. Renaming changes the slug too, and the foreign key carries every user on that role along with it — nobody is orphaned.

The built-in Admin role keeps its `admin` slug no matter what you call it, since the lockout guards name it.

**204** on success.

**409** when the role is built in, when users still hold it (the message counts them), or when deleting it would leave nobody able to manage roles at all.
Managing roles needs `role:create`, which only Admin holds out of the box. Run **Auth > Login as Viewer** once first.

item.name: Thundering herd (cache demo)
item.description:
**The problem.** A cached key expires or is invalidated. Every request that arrives before the first one finishes also sees a miss, so they *all* run the same query. 96 readers become 96 identical `SELECT`s — and it bites hardest exactly when traffic is highest.

**Why this is a server-side endpoint and not a Postman Runner loop.** Postman runs requests *sequentially* — request 2 does not leave until request 1 returns, so the misses never overlap and no herd ever forms. The burst has to be fired from one place at once, which is what `POST /diagnostics/thundering-herd` does with `Promise.all`.

**How to use this folder**

1. **Auth > Login as Admin** — these routes need `material:create` + `material:delete`.
2. Run **1. Reproduce**, note `database.listQueries`.
3. Run **2. Fixed**, note it again.
4. Open **4. Live dashboard** to see it on the graph.

**What the fix is:** single-flight (request coalescing) in `RedisService.remember` — the first miss runs the loader, every other request waits on that same promise. One query, N readers served.

---

### Three ways to do this in Postman

1. **Request "0. Burst"** — fires 100 concurrent calls from a pre-request script and reads the counters back. Self-contained, nothing to configure.
2. **Runner > Performance** — Postman's built-in load testing. Pick the collection, set virtual users and a duration, and it drives real concurrent traffic while charting response times. Use it against `GET /materials`; the cache card on the dashboard shows the effect.
3. **Requests "1." and "2."** — the server-side burst. Most precise, because the concurrency is created next to the cache instead of across a network, and it flips the fix per run without a restart.

**What does *not* work:** Runner with 100 iterations. That is sequential — request 2 leaves only after request 1 returns, so the misses never overlap and the herd never forms. You would see 100 cache hits and conclude, wrongly, that there is no problem.

exec: // Postman runs REQUESTS sequentially, but a script can still fire many
// calls at once — pm.sendRequest is async, so kicking off 100 of them and
// awaiting them together produces real concurrency inside one request.
pm.sendRequest({ url: base + path, method: method, header: auth },
// 1. start from a known state: zero the counters and drop the cached list,
//    so the burst lands on a cold key and every number belongs to this run
// 2. the burst itself — all N leave before any of them come back
pm.test("the whole burst reached the server", () =>
// With CACHE_SINGLEFLIGHT=true this is 1. Restart the API with
// CACHE_SINGLEFLIGHT=false and it jumps to ~N — that is the herd.

request.description:
Everything happens inside **this one Postman request**, no Runner needed.

**How it manages to be concurrent.** Postman runs *requests* one after another, but a script can fire many calls at once: `pm.sendRequest` is async, so starting 100 of them and awaiting them together means all 100 leave before any come back. That is genuine concurrency, from one process — the same shape that reproduces the herd.

**What the pre-request script does**

1. `POST /diagnostics/cache/reset` — zero the counters
2. `POST /diagnostics/cache/invalidate` — drop the cached list so the burst hits a cold key
3. fires `{{burstSize}}` concurrent `GET /materials`

The request itself then reads the counters back, so the **response is the proof**: `loads` is how many queries PostgreSQL actually saw.

**To see the problem instead of the fix**, restart the API with
`CACHE_SINGLEFLIGHT=false` and run this again — `loads` goes from 1 to roughly 100.

Measured here on 100 real HTTP requests:

| | DB loads | Wall clock | Completed |
| --- | --: | --: | --: |
| `CACHE_SINGLEFLIGHT=false` | 98 | 1098ms | 98 / 100 |
| `CACHE_SINGLEFLIGHT=true` | 1 | 97ms | 100 / 100 |

Note two requests did not even complete without the fix — the pool was saturated.

Change `{{burstSize}}` to try other numbers. Postman scripts have a time budget, so keep it in the hundreds.

Fires 96 concurrent reads with 3 writes spread through them. Each write invalidates the cached list, so the readers pile onto a cold key.

Expect `database.listQueries` around **96** — one per reader. That is the herd: the cache absorbed nothing and PostgreSQL took the whole burst.

Watch `cache.avgLoadMs` too — it climbs, because the queries are competing with each other for pool connections.

exec: console.log('WITHOUT fix -> ' + b.database.listQueries + ' db queries in ' + b.durationMs + 'ms');
pm.test('the herd happened: roughly one query per reader', () => pm.expect(b.database.listQueries).to.be.above(50));

request.description:
The same burst with coalescing on. The first miss runs the query; the other 95 wait on it.

Expect `database.listQueries` = **1** and `database.queriesAvoided` = 95. The duration falls with it, because the database is no longer serving 96 copies of one statement.

The test script prints both runs side by side in the Postman console.

exec: console.log('WITH fix    -> ' + b.database.listQueries + ' db queries in ' + b.durationMs + 'ms');
console.log('queries: ' + before + ' -> ' + b.database.listQueries + ' (' + Math.round(before / Math.max(1, b.database.listQueries)) + 'x fewer)');

request.description:
The raw counters, per key group.

- `loads` — times the loader ran, i.e. queries PostgreSQL saw
- `coalesced` — misses that waited on an in-flight load
- `hits` — served straight from Redis
- `invalidations` — keys dropped by a write

`auth:user:*` and `list:materials:*` are grouped, so one row covers every user and every filter combination.

Open this URL in a browser, not in Postman — it is an HTML page that streams over websockets.

The **Cache** card shows the four numbers as a bar chart plus a per-key table. Run request 1 and watch "DB loads" spike; run request 2 and watch "Queries avoided" take over instead.
Zeroes the cache counters so the next run starts clean.

The gap widens with scale: 500 readers still produce a handful of queries. Flip `singleFlight` to false to see 500 instead.

`reads` is capped at 1000 and `writes` at 50.

item.name: Metrics
item.description: The only routes outside RBAC. `dashboard.html` is opened straight in a browser tab and polls these with plain `fetch`, so there is nowhere to attach a bearer token. They expose request counts, not business data.

request.description:
One snapshot of everything the server has seen since it started (or since the last reset).

**totals** — `requests`, `success`, `failed`, split into `clientErrors` (4xx) and `serverErrors` (5xx), plus `successRate` / `failureRate` as percentages.

**load** — `inFlight` (requests being served right now), `peakInFlight`, `requestsPerMinute` (rolling 60-second window), `peakRequestsPerMinute`, and lifetime averages per minute and per second.

**latencyMs** — `average`, `min`, `max`, `p50`, `p95`, `p99`. Percentiles come from the last 1000 requests.

**byStatus** — a count per HTTP status code: `{ "200": 13, "400": 2, "404": 2 }`.

**byMethod** — a count per verb.

**byEndpoint** — per-route breakdown sorted by traffic, each with `hits`, `success`, `failed`, `successRate`, `avgMs`, `minMs`, `maxMs`, `lastStatus`. Numeric ids are collapsed, so `/materials/1` and `/materials/2` are counted together as `GET /api/materials/:id`.

**recentFailures** — the last 20 failures with the actual reason pulled out of the response body, whatever shape it used:
```
409  DELETE /api/categories/:id  -> This category has sub-categories. Delete those first.
400  POST /api/materials        -> uom: Unrecognized unit of measure; name: Material name is required
404  GET /api/does-not-exist     -> Cannot GET /api/does-not-exist
```

**slowestRequests** — the 10 slowest calls seen, with timestamps.

**process** — `pid`, node version, `heapUsedMb`, `rssMb`.

Also `uptime` (seconds + human readable) and `since` (when counting started).

Returns the dashboard HTML. Postman will show the raw markup — **open this URL in a browser instead**, e.g. http://localhost:3000/api/metrics/dashboard

The page connects over socket.io and updates the moment any API is hit, so it never needs refreshing. It shows:

- KPI tiles — total, successful, failed, requests/min, in-flight, average latency
- A live requests-per-second area chart over a rolling 60-second window, with hover crosshair and a table view
- Response counts by status class, and latency percentiles (p50 / p95 / p99)
- A per-endpoint table sorted by traffic
- The last 20 failures with their actual error message

Light and dark themes, plus a Reset button wired to `POST /metrics/reset`.

Clears every counter and restarts the uptime clock. Useful before a load test so the numbers only cover that run.

Returns `{ message, since }`.
Root route — returns the app's hello string. Handy for confirming the server is up and the `/api` prefix is applied.
